source.title: ByT5: Towards a Token-Free Future with Pre-trained Byte-to-Byte Models
source.authors: Lin-Ting Xue; Aditya Barua; Noah Constant; Rami Al-Rfou; Sharan Narang; Mihir Kale; Adam Roberts; Colin A. Raffel

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates downstream task scores across several model sizes, giving a conceptual test of downstream performance versus scale. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many downstream benchmark and ablation results. Rows below cover the complete model-size sweeps in Tables 2 and 3, which bear on V6. It does not report results on held-out pretraining loss, power-law fits, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Other downstream tables and ablation results are not evidence about those versions.
record.test_reason: A byte-vs-subword model paper, not a scaling study. Its own size sweeps (Small to XXL, about 300M to 12.9B parameters, fine-tuned) show whether downstream scores rise with scale, which bears on the 'improves with scale' part of V6. It fits no curves, does not test predictability or extrapolation, and never relates scores to pretraining loss. It cites Kaplan et al. only to set d_ff/d_model ≈ 2.5.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that ByT5 is competitive with parameter-matched mT5. It wins under 1B parameters, on generative, in-language multilingual and word-level tasks, and under noise. It slightly underperforms on English classification above 1B. Its gains come despite 4× less pretraining text, at the cost of more compute. They make no scaling-law claim.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares byte-level ByT5 with subword-level mT5 on downstream tasks; it does not use the original held-out-loss scaling-law measurement or fit its laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes differ by task and model family; ByT5 DROP scores dip at XL. The study does not assess sensitivity to scaling-law fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: At roughly matched parameter count, changing the ByT5 encoder/decoder depth split (36/12 vs 24/24 vs 12/36) moves downstream scores substantially: GEM-XSum 12.3 vs 7.1 vs 8.3, XNLI 78.3 vs 75.4 vs 73.5 (Table 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed parameter count, architecture shape (encoder/decoder depth split) can change downstream task performance substantially, especially for byte-level models; this concerns downstream metrics, not loss.

record.peer_reviewed: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: No held-out pretraining-loss measurements or scaling-law fits; downstream scores are reported without uncertainty estimates. The reported benchmark sweeps do not establish predictive extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: At the 60-row limit, omitted Table 4 cross-lingual benchmark scores, Table 5 word-level benchmark scores, Table 6 noise results, and Table 8 ablation results. These are downstream or robustness outcomes rather than held-out pretraining-loss scaling measurements; Table 4 and Table 5 contain additional downstream scores across sizes but were not extracted after retaining the complete Table 2 and Table 3 size sweeps.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss reported at any size.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation; all models are trained for a fixed 1M steps.
Shape ablations report downstream metrics only, not loss.
Text only; byte-level input is not another modality or training regime in the V5 sense.
Predictability (fitted trends, extrapolation) and the link between downstream scores and pretraining loss.
No exponent fits or fitting choices examined.

missing.what: ByT5 and mT5 size sweeps on word-level tasks. ByT5 is flat or non-monotonic (Dakshina CER 9.8, 9.9, 10.5, 10.6, 9.6; G2P WER 14.8, 14.0, 15.4, 14.7, 13.8). mT5 improves monotonically, with inflection accuracy 66.5→78.0.
XTREME size sweeps for mT5 and ByT5 (in-language, translate-train, zero-shot), e.g. ByT5 zero-shot WikiAnn is non-monotonic (57.6, 62.0, 61.6 …).

record.verdict_notes: The scale evidence is incidental: each family has only five sizes, there are no fits, and no uncertainty is reported. The mT5 size axis is confounded by vocabulary parameters (85% of Small, 16% of XXL). All models are trained for the same 1M steps, so compute and size grow together. Kaplan et al. is used only for the d_ff/d_model ratio.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of large-run held-out loss from fits on small runs.
Loss-minimizing parameter/token allocation at fixed compute, and its trend with compute.
Architecture effects on held-out loss at fixed parameter count; architecture ablations report downstream task metrics instead.
The paper reports downstream scores across model sizes, but does not fit predictive scaling curves, test extrapolation, or relate downstream scores to pretraining loss.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices or setup.

rows.subject: ByT5-Large
rows.check: ByT5 GEM-XSum rises only 11.1→11.5 from Base to Large, a small move in the right direction.

rows.subject: ByT5-XL
rows.check: ByT5 TweetQA rises only 70.0→70.6 from Large to XL, a marginal gain.

rows.subject: ByT5-XL
rows.note: Score decreases from the preceding size.
rows.check: State is correct (74.4→68.7 at XL). Note that the Small→XXL change is still a gain (66.6→80.0), so this is a single-step dip.

rows.subject: ByT5-XL
rows.note: Score decreases from the preceding size.
rows.check: State is correct (73.0→67.2 at XL). This is a single-step dip within an overall Small→XXL gain.

relationships.condition: mT5 and ByT5 fine-tuned on GLUE, SuperGLUE, GEM-XSum and TweetQA, plus mT5 on DROP, over five sizes
relationships.reason: Scores rise at every successive size: e.g. mT5 SuperGLUE 60.2→89.2 and ByT5 GEM-XSum 9.1→15.3 (R01–R48, R50–R58, R60). Some steps are small (R28, R39).
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased at every successive size, including mT5 SuperGLUE from 60.2 to 89.2 and ByT5 GEM-XSum from 9.1 to 15.3, although some gains were small.

relationships.condition: ByT5 on DROP, Large to XL
relationships.reason: DROP F1 falls 74.4→68.7 and EM falls 73.0→67.2 at XL, then recovers at XXL, so scores are not monotonic in size (R49, R59).
relationships.display_finding: At XL, F1 falls from 74.4 to 68.7 and exact match from 73.0 to 67.2 before recovering at XXL.

relationships.condition: ByT5 on word-level tasks (Dakshina, SIGMORPHON G2P), from Table 5 text
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not rows: ByT5 Dakshina CER worsens 9.8→10.6 from Small to XL, and G2P WER is non-monotonic (14.8, 14.0, 15.4, 14.7, 13.8). Scale brings little gain on these tasks.
relationships.display_finding: Dakshina CER worsens from 9.8 to 10.6 between Small and XL, while G2P WER varies non-monotonically through 14.8, 14.0, 15.4, 14.7, and 13.8.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: mT5 and ByT5 on GLUE, SuperGLUE, GEM-XSum, and TweetQA; reported successive sizes
reader_labels.reason: Scores increase at every successive size in these reported sweeps, supporting improvement with scale in these benchmark settings (R01–R40, excluding no rows).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ByT5 on DROP at XL compared with Large
reader_labels.reason: Both DROP F1 and EM fall at XL and then rise again at XXL, so downstream scores are not uniformly monotonic across the reported scale sweep (R49, R59).
